MOSCOW, Russia (CNN)  -- A passenger jet caught fire early Sunday, exploded and crashed into railway tracks in the central Russian city of Perm, killing all 88 people on board. Wreckage from the Aeroflot-Nord Boeing 737, which crashed near Perm, lies across a railway track. The exact cause of the pre-dawn crash is under investigation, but government spokesman Vladimir Markin said "a technical breakdown" was a likely cause. Markin said in televised remarks that the failure of one of the Boeing 737-500's two engines may have caused the plane to come down, The Associated Press reported. Airline officials have said there is no indication of terrorism. "We think it's very doubtful that it was the result of a terrorist attack, because at the scene, there were no traces of explosives as we know for now," said Lev Koshlyakov, Deputy Director General of Aeroflot. It took firefighters more than two hours to extinguish the blazing wreckage. When the sun rose, pieces of the Aeroflot jet were strewn about the railroad tracks. "It slammed in front of my house, and there was a huge flame," an unidentified woman in Perm told Russian state television. "It looked like fireworks." She said the impact of the crash "threw me across my sheets.... Then my daughter ran in from the next room and asked if a war had started." She and other witnesses said they saw the aircraft burning before it came crashing down. "It looked like a comet," she said. The jet was en route to Perm from Moscow when the pilots lost communication with air traffic control just before landing about 3:10 a.m. (2110 GMT), an Aeroflot official said. He described the weather at the time as "mediocre." The public safety minister for the Perm region said investigators were combing a 2.5-mile (4-kilometer) area, including homes and railways.  Watch more about the crash » . "Right now, it's apparent that there was a fire on the plane at one kilometer in the air," Yuri Orlov said. "After that, all contact was cut off -- the plane exploded." The flight data recorder has been recovered and will be analyzed by the International Aviation Commission, Russian Transport Minister Igor Levitin said. The plane carried 82 passengers, including seven children, and a crew of six. At least 21 non-Russians were on board, including passport-holders from Azerbaijan, Germany, France, Italy, Switzerland and Ukraine, said Lev Koshlyakov, Aeroflot's deputy director general. The U.S. Embassy confirmed that no Americans were on board the flight, even though one passenger was listed as a U.S. citizen. It is the second crash in the region involving a Boeing 737 in less than a month. An Iran-bound Boeing 737 with 90 people on board crashed on August 24 just outside the airport in Kyrgyzstan's capital, Bishkek, killing 68. The 737 is a workhorse of the airline industry, with thousands of planes in service. Aeroflot said the one that crashed in Perm was manufactured in 1992 and was operated by its Aeroflot-Nord subsidiary. "This Boeing 737 has all the necessary certificates," Koshlyakov said. "We conduct audits and inspections of all the affiliate companies we work with in the realm of their effectiveness, safety and reliability of the airplanes." Airline safety in Russia and the former Soviet Union is among the worst in the world. Aviation experts say poor maintenance, inadequate pilot training and weak government controls are major factors. But Aeroflot is considered one of the safer airlines in the region. Sunday's crash is the first fatal accident for the airline since 1994, when a Russian pilot handed control of an Airbus to his 15-year-old son. It crashed, killing all 75 people on board. Russia's government has now ordered an inquiry into the latest incident, to find out how another routine flight could have ended in tragedy. The National Transportation Safety Board will send a team of investigators to Perm to look into the incident -- a standard practice when a U.S.-made aircraft crashes. CNN's Kathleen Koch and Michael Sefanov contributed to this report .

MOSCOW, Russia (CNN) — A passenger jet caught fire early Sunday, exploded, and crashed onto railway tracks in the central Russian city of Perm, killing all 88 people on board.

Wreckage from the Aeroflot-Nord Boeing 737 lay scattered across a railway track near Perm.

The exact cause of the pre-dawn crash remains under investigation, but government spokesman Vladimir Markin said “a technical breakdown” was a likely cause. In televised remarks, Markin said the failure of one of the Boeing 737-500’s two engines may have brought down the aircraft, The Associated Press reported.

Airline officials said there was no indication of terrorism.

“We think it’s very doubtful that it was the result of a terrorist attack, because at the scene, there were no traces of explosives as we know for now,” said Lev Koshlyakov, deputy director general of Aeroflot.

Firefighters took more than two hours to extinguish the blazing wreckage. By sunrise, pieces of the Aeroflot jet were strewn across the railroad tracks.

“It slammed in front of my house, and there was a huge flame,” an unidentified woman in Perm told Russian state television. “It looked like fireworks.”

She said the impact of the crash “threw me across my sheets.... Then my daughter ran in from the next room and asked if a war had started.”

She and other witnesses said they saw the aircraft burning before it crashed.

“It looked like a comet,” she said.

The jet was traveling from Moscow to Perm when the pilots lost communication with air traffic control shortly before landing, at about 3:10 a.m. (2110 GMT), an Aeroflot official said. He described the weather at the time as “mediocre.”

The public safety minister for the Perm region said investigators were combing a 2.5-mile (4-kilometer) area that included homes and railways.

“Right now, it’s apparent that there was a fire on the plane at one kilometer in the air,” Yuri Orlov said. “After that, all contact was cut off—the plane exploded.”

The flight data recorder was recovered and will be analyzed by the International Aviation Commission, Russian Transport Minister Igor Levitin said.

The aircraft was carrying 82 passengers, including seven children, and a crew of six. At least 21 non-Russians were on board, including passport holders from Azerbaijan, Germany, France, Italy, Switzerland, and Ukraine, Koshlyakov said.

The U.S. Embassy confirmed that no Americans were aboard the flight, although one passenger had been listed as a U.S. citizen.

The accident was the second crash in the region involving a Boeing 737 in less than a month. On August 24, an Iran-bound Boeing 737 carrying 90 people crashed just outside the airport in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, killing 68.

The 737 is a workhorse of the airline industry, with thousands of aircraft in service. Aeroflot said the plane that crashed in Perm was manufactured in 1992 and operated by its Aeroflot-Nord subsidiary.

“This Boeing 737 has all the necessary certificates,” Koshlyakov said. “We conduct audits and inspections of all the affiliate companies we work with in the realm of their effectiveness, safety and reliability of the airplanes.”

Airline safety in Russia and the former Soviet Union ranks among the worst in the world. Aviation experts cite poor maintenance, inadequate pilot training, and weak government oversight as major factors. Aeroflot, however, is considered one of the safer airlines in the region.

Sunday’s crash was the airline’s first fatal accident since 1994, when a Russian pilot handed control of an Airbus to his 15-year-old son. The aircraft crashed, killing all 75 people on board.

The Russian government has ordered an inquiry into the latest incident to determine how another routine flight ended in tragedy.

The National Transportation Safety Board will send a team of investigators to Perm to examine the incident—a standard practice when a U.S.-made aircraft crashes.

CNN’s Kathleen Koch and Michael Sefanov contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
**MOSCOW, Russia (CNN) —** All 88 people aboard a passenger aircraft died early Sunday after the jet caught fire, exploded and fell onto railroad tracks in Perm, a city in central Russia.

Debris from the Aeroflot-Nord Boeing 737 was scattered across the railway line near the crash site. Authorities were still working to determine what caused the accident, though Russian government spokesman Vladimir Markin said a mechanical malfunction appeared likely. In televised comments, Markin suggested that one of the Boeing 737-500’s two engines may have failed, according to The Associated Press.

Aeroflot officials said they had found nothing pointing to terrorism. Lev Koshlyakov, the airline’s deputy director general, said a terrorist attack appeared highly unlikely because, based on the information available at the time, investigators had discovered no evidence of explosives.

Fire crews needed more than two hours to put out the burning remains. By daylight, fragments of the aircraft could be seen spread over the tracks.

A Perm resident, whose name was not given, told Russian state television that the plane struck the ground in front of her home and produced an enormous burst of fire resembling fireworks. She said the force of the impact tossed her across her bed. Her daughter then rushed in from another room and asked whether a war had begun.

The woman and other eyewitnesses reported seeing the aircraft on fire before it hit the ground. She compared its appearance to a comet.

The flight was traveling from Moscow to Perm. At approximately 3:10 a.m. local time Sunday, or 2110 GMT, shortly before the scheduled landing, the pilots lost contact with air traffic controllers, according to an Aeroflot official. He characterized the weather conditions as “mediocre.”

Yuri Orlov, the Perm region’s public safety minister, said search teams were examining an area extending 2.5 miles, or 4 kilometers, and covering both residential property and railway lines. He said the available evidence indicated that the aircraft caught fire while about one kilometer above the ground. Communication then ended, and the jet exploded.

Russian Transport Minister Igor Levitin announced that the flight data recorder had been found. It was to be examined by the International Aviation Commission.

The aircraft was carrying 82 passengers—including seven children—as well as six crew members. Koshlyakov said at least 21 passengers were not Russian citizens. Among them were people holding passports from Azerbaijan, Germany, France, Italy, Switzerland and Ukraine.

Although one name on the passenger list was identified as belonging to a U.S. citizen, the U.S. Embassy said no Americans had been aboard.

The disaster was the second involving a Boeing 737 in the region in less than one month. On August 24, another 737, bound for Iran with 90 occupants, crashed near the airport serving Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan. Sixty-eight people died in that accident.

Thousands of Boeing 737s are in operation, making the model one of the aviation industry’s most widely used aircraft. Aeroflot said the jet lost near Perm had been built in 1992 and was flown by its Aeroflot-Nord subsidiary.

Koshlyakov said the aircraft possessed every required certification. He added that Aeroflot audits and inspects its affiliated companies to evaluate their performance, safety standards and the reliability of their fleets.

Russia and other former Soviet republics have some of the world’s poorest airline-safety records. Aviation specialists frequently identify insufficient maintenance, weak pilot instruction and ineffective government oversight as leading causes. Aeroflot, however, is regarded as one of the region’s safer carriers.

Sunday’s accident was Aeroflot’s first fatal crash since 1994. In that earlier incident, a Russian pilot allowed his 15-year-old son to take the controls of an Airbus. The aircraft crashed, killing all 75 people aboard.

The Russian government ordered an investigation into the latest tragedy to establish why an otherwise routine journey ended in disaster. The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board also planned to dispatch investigators to Perm, as is customary when an American-manufactured aircraft is involved in a crash.

CNN’s Kathleen Koch and Michael Sefanov contributed to the report.

counterfactuals.output:
## Passenger jet crashes in Russia, killing all 88 aboard

**PERM, Russia (CNN) —** A Boeing 737 operated by Aeroflot-Nord crashed near the Russian city of Perm early September 14, 2008, killing all 88 people on board, Russian authorities said.

Flight 821 was traveling from Moscow to Perm with 82 passengers and six crew members when it went down during its approach to Perm’s airport. There were no survivors.

The aircraft struck the ground near a residential area and a section of the Trans-Siberian Railway, scattering burning wreckage across a wide area and temporarily disrupting rail service. No casualties were reported on the ground.

Witnesses told Russian media they heard a loud roar before seeing the aircraft descend at a steep angle. Some described a flash or fireball followed by a powerful explosion that shook nearby buildings. Investigators cautioned that such accounts did not necessarily mean there had been an explosion or fire aboard the plane before impact.

Initial speculation focused on a possible engine problem, poor weather and mechanical failure. Officials said the aircraft had been flying at night in cloud and rain, conditions that offered the pilots few visual references.

Russia’s Interstate Aviation Committee later concluded that the crew lost control after the autopilot was disconnected during the approach. The final report said the captain became spatially disoriented and made control inputs that sent the aircraft into a steep bank and rapid descent.

Investigators cited several contributing factors, including inadequate pilot training, poor crew coordination and difficulties transitioning between Soviet-designed aircraft and the Western-style cockpit instruments used in the Boeing 737. Toxicology testing also found alcohol in the captain’s system, and investigators said his condition contributed to the accident.

Flight data and cockpit voice recorders were recovered from the wreckage and used to reconstruct the aircraft’s final minutes. The investigation also examined Aeroflot-Nord’s training, supervision and safety practices.

Aeroflot-Nord was a regional carrier operating the flight under an agreement with Aeroflot. Following the crash, Aeroflot moved to distance its brand from the airline, which was later renamed Nordavia.

The disaster was one of Russia’s deadliest aviation accidents in the years following the collapse of the Soviet Union and prompted renewed scrutiny of pilot training and oversight at regional carriers.

President Dmitry Medvedev and Prime Minister Vladimir Putin offered condolences, and a day of mourning was declared locally.

**September 15, 2008**

# Flight Data Recorder Recovered After Perm Airliner Crash Kills 88

**PERM, Russia** — Investigators recovered the flight data recorder Monday from the wreckage of an Aeroflot-Nord passenger jet that crashed near the Ural Mountains city of Perm, killing all 88 people aboard.

The Boeing 737-500, operating as Aeroflot Flight 821, went down early Sunday while approaching Perm at the end of a flight from Moscow. The aircraft struck a railway embankment in a residential area on the outskirts of the city, scattering burning debris over a wide area and damaging a section of the Trans-Siberian Railway.

“There were no survivors,” Vladimir Markin, a spokesman for Russia’s Investigative Committee, told Russian news agencies.

The aircraft was carrying 82 passengers and six crew members. No one on the ground was reported killed, despite the crash occurring within the city limits and close to apartment buildings.

Emergency workers found the flight data recorder, commonly called a “black box,” amid the wreckage. Officials said it would be sent to specialists from Russia’s Interstate Aviation Committee for examination. Investigators hoped it would provide crucial information about the aircraft’s speed, altitude, heading and engine performance during the final minutes of the flight.

Authorities also searched the site for cockpit recordings and other evidence. Officials cautioned that the recovered equipment had been exposed to severe impact forces and fire.

## Aircraft Lost Contact During Approach

Russian aviation officials said the jet disappeared from radar shortly after air traffic controllers instructed the crew to make another approach to Perm’s Bolshoye Savino Airport.

“The aircraft lost communication with the ground at an altitude of about 1,800 metres,” aviation official Gennady Kurzenkov said in remarks carried by Russian media.

The crew had not reported an emergency before contact was lost, according to initial statements. Officials said investigators were examining several possibilities, including technical failure, pilot error and poor coordination during the approach. They stressed that it was too early to identify a cause.

The aircraft’s debris was spread along a broad path, and the crash tore up hundreds of metres of railway track. Train traffic through the area was temporarily suspended while repair crews and investigators worked at the scene.

## Witnesses Report Flash and Explosion

Residents near the crash site described being awakened by a low-flying aircraft, followed by a flash and a powerful explosion.

“I heard a roar, and then there was a bright flash,” one local resident told Russian television. “A few seconds later, there was an explosion.”

Another witness said the aircraft appeared to be flying unusually low over the neighborhood before it struck the ground. Several residents said windows shook from the blast and that flames could be seen above the railway line.

Some early witness accounts suggested the aircraft may have been burning before impact. Investigators said those reports had not yet been confirmed and warned against drawing conclusions before the flight recorder data and wreckage were analyzed.

Firefighters extinguished the main blaze, while rescue teams searched through twisted metal, luggage and personal belongings. The force of the crash and subsequent fire made identification of the victims difficult, prompting authorities to request DNA samples from relatives.

## Senior Officials Sent to Perm

President Dmitry Medvedev ordered a full investigation, and Prime Minister Vladimir Putin established a government commission to coordinate the response. Transport Minister Igor Levitin and Emergencies Minister Sergei Shoigu traveled to Perm to oversee work at the site and meet regional officials.

Shoigu said emergency personnel were concentrating on recovering victims, securing wreckage and restoring the damaged railway.

Prosecutors opened a criminal investigation under statutes covering violations of air-transport safety rules. Such investigations are standard after major Russian aviation accidents.

Aeroflot-Nord, a regional airline using the Aeroflot name under a commercial agreement, said the aircraft had passed required maintenance checks. The jet, built in 1992, had previously been operated by foreign carriers before entering service in Russia.

Aeroflot said in a statement that it expressed “deep condolences to the relatives and friends of those killed” and would assist the victims’ families.

The passenger list included several foreign nationals as well as Russian citizens. Among those killed was Gen. Gennady Troshev, a former senior Russian commander who had served in the wars in Chechnya.

Perm regional authorities declared a period of mourning. Residents brought flowers and candles to a memorial near the crash area as relatives arrived from Moscow and other cities seeking information.

Investigators said a preliminary assessment could take weeks, while a final determination of the cause would depend on analysis of the flight recorder, air traffic control communications, weather information, crew records and the damaged aircraft systems.

counterfactuals.prompt: What happened in the fatal 2008 Boeing 737 crash near Perm, and what did investigators, Aeroflot representatives, and local witnesses initially say about it?
counterfactuals.output:
On 14 September 2008, Aeroflot‑Nord Flight 821, a Boeing 737‑500 flying from Moscow to Perm, lost control during a nighttime approach to Perm’s Bolshoye Savino Airport. The aircraft entered a steep, banked descent and struck a railway embankment on the outskirts of the city, breaking up and burning. All 88 people aboard—82 passengers and six crew—were killed, and part of the Trans‑Siberian Railway was damaged.

**Initial accounts:**

- **Investigators and air-traffic officials** said contact was lost while the jet was approaching at roughly 1,100 metres. The crew had been instructed to discontinue the approach and go around, but the aircraft turned and descended abnormally. Early evidence suggested it was intact until impact; officials initially found no indication of terrorism or an in‑flight explosion, although the flight recorders were badly damaged.
- **Aeroflot/Aeroflot‑Nord representatives** initially said the aircraft had been technically serviceable, the weather was suitable for landing, and the crew had not transmitted a clear distress call before it disappeared from radar. They cautioned that the cause was still unknown.
- **Local witnesses** described the jet flying very low, making unusual turns, and then crashing with a powerful flash or explosion that shook nearby buildings. Some said they saw flames or believed the aircraft was already on fire, but those observations were not ultimately accepted as proof of an in‑flight fire.

The later official investigation concluded that the principal cause was **loss of spatial orientation and control by the crew during the go‑around**, compounded by inadequate training and cockpit coordination. Toxicology also found alcohol in the captain’s system. Investigators did not find a pre-impact mechanical failure or fire that caused the crash.
